en: **Aṣṭamahācaityavandanā** **Author:** King Harṣa **Source:** Lévi 1894 (Sanskrit text restored from the Chinese transcription by Fa-t'ien); also cf. *Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha*, no. 22. *(Note: This work is a hymn of praise to the eight great caityas of Buddhism.)*
Birth, supreme enlightenment, and the incomparable, delightful Wheel of Dharma—

I bow with my head prostrated to the primordial shrine, the glorious Great Miracle honored by the three worlds, and to this place, the abode on the Snowy Mountain where the God of Gods descended and where the Buddhas attained final liberation.

I pay homage with devotion to the Buddha at Vaiśālī, at the Wheel of Dharma, on the slope of Śiṣumāragiri, on the bank of the Bhīṣmaka, at Śrāvastī, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, in the excellent city of Kuśinagara, and at Lumbinī and Kapilavastu.

I bow my head in homage to the Teacher’s shrines located in the city of Āne-kāpila, in Kauśāmbī at Smerakoṣṭha, in the excellent city of Mathurā, in the realm of Nandagopa, and to whatever other shrines of the Teacher exist, who is endowed with the power of the Ten Strengths.
[There are] reliquaries of the Teacher, O Queen, or reliquaries of the relics,
in Kaśmīra, in the land of Cīna, on the banks of the Khaṣa and Yamunā, in Marvāra, or in Siṃhala; in Lāṭa, Uḍra, Sindhupauṇḍra, Samataṭa, Magadha, Mekhala, or Kosala.
in Barbara, in Nepal, in Kāmarūpa, in the excellent city of Kalaśa, and in the kingdoms of Kāñcī and Saurāṣṭra—
And those others who possess the essence of the elements and are endowed with the power of the ten strengths—to them I bow my head in homage.

[4] O Ānanda, there are relic-stūpas on Kailāsa, Hemakūṭa, and the abode of the Snowy Mountain; on Mandara, on the peak of Meru, in Pātāla, in Vaijayanta the abode of the Lord of Wealth, and in the world of the Siddhas and Gandharvas.
In the cosmic egg, on the earth of Viṣṇu, in the abode of Paśupati, in the worlds of the moon, the sun, and so forth—
whosoever else there are who possess the essence of the elements and are endowed with the power of the Ten Forces, to them I bow my head.

The relic-caityas of the Buddha, those eight containing relics of the One Endowed with the Ten Powers, the caityas known as "the Jar," as well as others called "the Charcoal," which resemble snow and silver and shine like jewels upon stupas; [5] all these...

Those [images] in the netherworld, those upon the earth, and those situated on mountain peaks— everywhere, those images of the Buddhas containing all the elements— I bow my head to them repeatedly every day.
... which are they? [They are] those others... Thus ends the *Aṣṭamahāsthānacaityavandanā*.
